transcript.text: The sides of our new fridge freezer get really warm, almost hot, especially near the front edge. Is that a fire risk? It's in an alcove between two units.

Usually, no: warm—sometimes very warm—side panels and the front edges are normal on many fridge freezers. They use the cabinet walls/front frame to shed heat, so this is often most noticeable when the compressor is working hard, especially on a new appliance settling in. The alcove is the important part. If heat cannot escape around the appliance, the sides can become unusually hot and it has to run longer. Check these points: 1. Check the installation guide for the required gaps at the sides, rear and above. Do not assume a tight built-in-style fit is suitable unless the appliance is designed for it. If the gaps are smaller than specified, pull it forward or improve ventilation. 2. Make sure the rear and any ventilation grilles are not blocked by the wall, units, packaging or dust. Switch off and unplug it before moving or cleaning; avoid trapping the mains lead. 3. Leave it running with doors mostly shut for 24 hours, then check it is cooling normally: fridge about 3–5°C and freezer about -18°C. A new fridge freezer can take up to a day to settle. Warm sides alone are not normally a fire-risk sign. Stop using it and contact the retailer/manufacturer promptly if the casing is too hot to keep your hand on, there is a burning smell, smoke, repeated tripping of the electrics, damaged plug/lead, or it is not cooling properly. If it remains excessively hot despite the specified ventilation space, it needs checking under warranty rather than being used tightly enclosed.

Thanks. I can keep my hand on it, it's warm like a radiator on low, not too hot to touch. There's no burning smell either. The gaps are only about 1cm each side and a few cm above, and I'd rather not pull it out as the floor is new. The temperatures read 4C and -18C. Is that gap tight enough to be a problem?

It could be. A 1cm side gap is tight for many freestanding fridge freezers, although it is acceptable for some models; the required clearance is model-specific. Because it is holding 4°C in the fridge and -18°C in the freezer, and the panels are only low-radiator warm with no burning smell, this does not currently sound like a fire-risk fault. The warm front edges/sides are most likely normal heat being shed from the cooling system. In a tight alcove, though, that heat has less air to escape into, so the appliance may run longer and feel warmer. 1. Check the installation instructions or the retailer’s product page for the stated side, top and rear gaps. That is the deciding figure—not a generic rule. If it specifies more than 1cm at the sides, the fit is too tight even if it is cooling correctly.
2. Check that there is a clear route for warm air at the rear and above: no packaging, end panels or cupboards sealing it in. You need not drag it across the new floor just to do this; a torch from above or alongside may be enough.
3. Over the next day or two, keep an eye on the temperatures. Staying around 3–5°C and -18°C, without the casing becoming too hot to hold, supports normal operation. If the manual requires larger gaps, it is worth having the retailer/installer advise on ventilation rather than leaving it tightly enclosed. Stop use and contact them promptly if it becomes too hot to keep your hand on, develops a burning smell, trips electrics, or stops maintaining temperature.
I have the manual here (model H7X 93T SK) but I didn't check the clearances exactly, it just says to leave space. What should I look for in it?

Look for a section headed “Installation”, “Positioning”, “Ventilation”, “Location” or “Dimensions” — often there is a small cabinet diagram rather than a sentence in the main text. 1. Minimum gaps at the sides, above and behind the appliance. These may be shown in mm, for example as arrows around a drawing.
2. Any instruction that ventilation openings must not be obstructed, or that it must not be enclosed in a recess/alcove.
3. Whether it distinguishes between a freestanding appliance and an integrated/built-in installation. A freestanding fridge freezer generally must not be treated as built-in unless the instructions specifically allow it.
4. The climate class / permitted room-temperature range. This is less likely to explain the warm sides, but is worth noting if the alcove is in a hot room. The deciding point is the stated clearance, especially at the rear and above where warm air needs an escape route. If you can give the figures from that diagram or section, I can help interpret whether the alcove fit meets them.
Ok, I'll have a look through it for the diagram. Just to be clear, there's no burning smell or scorching, and nothing has tripped. Is there anything else I should check while I find that section?

Other than finding the stated clearances, there is no need to dismantle or move anything at this point. The temperatures are correct and the warmth is touch-safe, with no smell, scorching or electrical tripping, so normal heat being shed through the cabinet remains the most likely explanation. While you have the manual out, two useful non-invasive checks are:
1. Use a torch to look down behind/above it, without pulling it out: check no packaging, loose item, unit panel or wall is closing off any rear or top ventilation route. If warm air has nowhere to rise and escape, the cabinet can run warmer and for longer.
2. Have a quick look at the plug and visible lead only: they should be undamaged, not trapped or tightly kinked, and the plug/socket should not feel hot. A slightly warm plug can occur under load, but hot plastic, discolouration or a loose socket would mean stop using it and contact the retailer or an electrician. The deciding check is still the installation diagram. Once you have the minimum side, rear and top figures, compare them with the roughly 1 cm at the sides and few centimetres above. If the manual calls for more space, ask the retailer/installer how they propose to ventilate the alcove rather than forcing the appliance out yourself.
Plug and socket aren't warm, and I can't see any damage on the lead. I'll go through the manual for the diagram and come back with the figures. Is there anything else you need from me?

No—nothing further is essential at the moment beyond the installation-clearance figures. The one thing that will settle whether the alcove is suitable is the manual’s minimum side, rear and top gaps. Please send those figures when you find them; a photo or the wording from the diagram is fine. If the diagram is unclear, the only other useful observation is whether there is an open route for warm air to rise out at the rear/top of the alcove, rather than the space being sealed in by the surrounding units. You do not need to pull the appliance out or dismantle anything to check that.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
